messages.author: 353e4f85443252a1
messages.subject: Right-truncated gamma
parts:
Hi,

Is there a possibility to fit an INLA model that uses a right-truncated
gamma distribution, or to do something similar to that?

The case at hand is a hurdle gamma model for phreatic groundwater depth
in wetlands. The gamma part should probably be truncated since this
response, 'by nature', will never be larger than, say, 10 or 20 meter
(in the dataset, the maximum is below 3.5 meter anyway). The fitted
hurdle gamma model is sensible, except that when simulating numerous
data, occasional values even above 100 meter do occur, i.e. far outside
the realistic range.

Kind regards

Floris

messages.author: 936ef8c6d12fc338
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Right-truncated gamma
parts:
Hi Floris,

When the problem is only in the simulated values, you could simply truncate the simulated values. I don't expect to model parameters to be different when you truncate the distribution at a level outside the range of the data.

Maybe you could rescale the response to the [0, 1] interval and use a beta distribution with added point masses at 0 and 1.

Best regards,

messages.author: 353e4f85443252a1
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Right-truncated gamma
parts:
Thank you for these suggestions Thierry.

Tried truncation of simulated data, truncating at value 10. If I understand you right, you mean replacing values > 10 by value 10 (right-censoring); at least that's below approach—an alternative might be to replace them with new simulated values, i.e. discard extremes. In the log-scale, the artificial effect becomes a bit more apparent, but it seems still acceptable to me.


Rescaling to prepare for a beta distribution and adding an extra bernouilli submodel to include the value of 1 may be a good alternative, but indeed it may be unnecessary in this case.

Kind regards

Floris

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Right-truncated gamma
parts:
Thanks! I've never been into survival modelling, but will have a look
how this fits in.

Regarding the route of 'truncating simulated data', it's probably most
elegant to truncate the gamma density function first, and then simulate
from that. E.g.
https://www.r-bloggers.com/2020/08/generating-data-from-a-truncated-distribution/.
I think it's equivalent with dropping too extreme data and replacing
them with new values, but does it more directly.

Floris

'inla.surv' to define an event in an interval

messages.author: 353e4f85443252a1
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Right-truncated gamma
parts:
The source of the problem in the usecase is more complex it seems, than my initial thought about the width of the gamma distribution.

From closer inspection of the extreme simulated observations (above value 10), it appears that two sources contribute to ± the same extent in generating extreme responses (which represent about 0.2% of the total simulated observations):

  • the linear predictor LPi of the gamma submodel (the gamma mean being exp(LPi)), so this is another obvious source. The extreme values at this level are all caused by extreme sampled values from either of three gaussian distributions, i.e. corresponding to three iid random effects
  • the gamma distribution itself, as discussed before

Maybe truncating the four involved distributions (3 x gaussian, 1 x gamma), when simulating, would be a fine solution, but first will have a look how inla.surv may help.

Floris
